subject: Ergocalciferol
object: tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding
relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

Omeprazole may also be given together with antibiotics to treat gastric ulcers caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), in adult patients.
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by blocking the acid pump in your stomach, reducing how much acid it makes and giving irritated or damaged tissue a chance to heal.
Omeprazole brand names are Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic brands are available.
Omeprazole is available over the counter (OTC) and as a prescription medication.

subject: omeprazole
relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
evidence_text:
Omeprazole usually takes 1 to 4 days of once-daily dosing to reach its full effect, and some people get complete relief of their symptoms within 24 hours. It begins reducing stomach acid within about 1 hour of the first dose, but it is not designed to relieve heartburn right away.
What to expect after you start taking omeprazole:
- Within 1 hour: omeprazole starts to reduce acid production in your stomach
- Around 2 hours: a single dose reaches its strongest acid-lowering effect
- Within 24 hours: some people get complete relief of their symptoms
- 1 to 4 days: most people feel the full benefit
- About 4 days: the acid-lowering effect reaches its maximum with once-daily dosing
How fast does omeprazole start working?:
Omeprazole starts working within about 1 hour, and a single dose has its strongest effect at around 2 hours. This is when the medicine begins lowering acid production, which is not the same as when your heartburn or acid reflux symptoms stop.

Omeprazole is used to treat excess stomach acid in conditions such as stomach ulcers, heartburn or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), active duodenal ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and erosive esophagitis.
Omeprazole may also be given together with antibiotics to treat gastric ulcers caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), in adult patients.
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by blocking the acid pump in your stomach, reducing how much acid it makes and giving irritated or damaged tissue a chance to heal.
Omeprazole brand names are Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic brands are available.
Omeprazole is available over the counter (OTC) and as a prescription medication.

- Within 1 hour: omeprazole starts to reduce acid production in your stomach
- Around 2 hours: a single dose reaches its strongest acid-lowering effect
- Within 24 hours: some people get complete relief of their symptoms
- 1 to 4 days: most people feel the full benefit
- About 4 days: the acid-lowering effect reaches its maximum with once-daily dosing

object: give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you
relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
evidence_text:
Ondansetron can cause a serious heart problem, especially if you use certain medicines at the same time, including antibiotics, antidepressants, heart rhythm medicine, antipsychotic medicines, and medicines to treat cancer, malaria, HIV or AIDS. Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment with ondansetron.
Taking ondansetron while you are using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body, a condition called "serotonin syndrome," which can be fatal. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine to treat depression;
- medicine to treat a psychiatric disorder;
- a narcotic (opioid) medication; or
- medicine to prevent nausea and vomiting.
This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with ondansetron. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
evidence_text:
Take ondansetron exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
Ondansetron can be taken with or without food.
The first dose is usually taken before the start of your surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation treatment. Follow your doctor's dosing instructions very carefully.
Take the ondansetron regular tablet with a full glass of water.
To take the orally disintegrating tablet (Zofran ODT):
- Keep the tablet in its blister pack until you are ready to take it. Open the package and peel back the foil. Do not push a tablet through the foil or you may damage the tablet.
- Use dry hands to remove the tablet and place it in your mouth.
- Do not swallow the tablet whole. Allow it to dissolve in your mouth without chewing.
- Swallow several times as the tablet dissolves.
To use ondansetron oral soluble film (strip) (Zuplenz):
- Keep the strip in the foil pouch until you are ready to use the medicine.

subject: ondansetron
object: tell your doctor about all medicines you use
relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
evidence_text:
Ondansetron can cause a serious heart problem, especially if you use certain medicines at the same time, including antibiotics, antidepressants, heart rhythm medicine, antipsychotic medicines, and medicines to treat cancer, malaria, HIV or AIDS. Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment with ondansetron.
Taking ondansetron while you are using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body, a condition called "serotonin syndrome," which can be fatal. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine to treat depression;
- medicine to treat a psychiatric disorder;
- a narcotic (opioid) medication; or
- medicine to prevent nausea and vomiting.
This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with ondansetron. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

subject: ondansetron
object: not expected to harm an unborn baby
relation_definition: The subject drug carries the warning specified by the object entity regarding use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
evidence_text:
You should not use ondansetron if:
- you are also using apomorphine (Apokyn); or
- you are allergic to ondansetron or similar medicines (dolasetron, granisetron, palonosetron).
To make sure ondansetron is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have:
- liver disease;
- an electrolyte imbalance (such as low levels of potassium or magnesium in your blood);
- congestive heart failure, slow heartbeats;
- a personal or family history of long QT syndrome; or
- a blockage in your digestive tract (stomach or intestines).
Ondansetron is not expected to harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant.
It is not known whether ondansetron passes into breast milk or if it could harm a nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding a baby.
Ondansetron is not approved for use by anyone younger than 1 month old.
Ondansetron orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Tell your doctor if you have phenylketonuria (PKU).

evidence_text:
Take pantoprazole exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Use the lowest dose for the shortest amount of time needed to treat your condition.
Pantoprazole is taken by mouth (oral) or given as an infusion into a vein (injection). A healthcare provider may teach you how to properly use the injection by yourself.
Pantoprazole tablets are taken by mouth, with or without food. The oral granules should be taken 30 minutes before a meal.
Do not crush, chew, or break the tablet or oral granules. Swallow the tablet whole.

Use this medicine for the full prescribed length of time, even if your symptoms quickly improve.

evidence_text:
Pantoprazole is not for the immediate relief of heartburn symptoms.
Heartburn is often confused with the first symptoms of a heart attack. Seek emergency medical attention if you have chest pain or heavy feeling, pain spreading to the arm or shoulder, nausea, sweating, and a general ill feeling.
Long-term treatment with pantoprazole may also make it harder for your body to absorb vitamin B-12, resulting in a deficiency of this vitamin. Talk with your doctor if you need long-term pantoprazole treatment and you have concerns about vitamin B-12 deficiency.
Pantoprazole can cause kidney problems. Tell your doctor if you are urinating less than usual, or if you have blood in your urine.
Diarrhea may be a sign of a new infection. Call your doctor if you have diarrhea that is watery or has blood in it.
Pantoprazole may cause new or worsening symptoms of lupus. Tell your doctor if you have joint pain and a skin rash on your cheeks or arms that worsens in sunlight.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while taking this medicine long term or more than once per day.

evidence_text:
Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that decreases the amount of acid produced in the stomach.
Pantoprazole is used to treat erosive esophagitis (damage to the esophagus from stomach acid caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD) in adults and children who are at least 5 years old. Pantoprazole is usually given for up to 8 weeks at a time while your esophagus heals.
Pantoprazole is also used to treat Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and other conditions involving excess stomach acid.

Pantoprazole is not for the immediate relief of heartburn symptoms.
Heartburn is often confused with the first symptoms of a heart attack. Seek emergency medical attention if you have chest pain or heavy feeling, pain spreading to the arm or shoulder, nausea, sweating, and a general ill feeling.
Long-term treatment with pantoprazole may also make it harder for your body to absorb vitamin B-12, resulting in a deficiency of this vitamin. Talk with your doctor if you need long-term pantoprazole treatment and you have concerns about vitamin B-12 deficiency.
Pantoprazole can cause kidney problems. Tell your doctor if you are urinating less than usual, or if you have blood in your urine.
Diarrhea may be a sign of a new infection. Call your doctor if you have diarrhea that is watery or has blood in it.
Pantoprazole may cause new or worsening symptoms of lupus. Tell your doctor if you have joint pain and a skin rash on your cheeks or arms that worsens in sunlight.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while taking this medicine long term or more than once per day.

Taking pantoprazole long-term may cause you to develop stomach growths called fundic gland polyps. Talk with your doctor about this risk.
If you use pantoprazole for longer than 3 years, you could develop a vitamin B-12 deficiency. Talk to your doctor about how to manage this condition if you develop it.
Common pantoprazole side effects may include:
- headache, dizziness;
- stomach pain, gas, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- joint pain; or
- fever, rash, or cold symptoms (most common in children).
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that decreases the amount of acid produced in the stomach.
Pantoprazole is used to treat erosive esophagitis (damage to the esophagus from stomach acid caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD) in adults and children who are at least 5 years old. Pantoprazole is usually given for up to 8 weeks at a time while your esophagus heals.
Pantoprazole is also used to treat Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and other conditions involving excess stomach acid.

subject: Potassium Chloride
relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe throat irritation;
- stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
- high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
- signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.

relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.

If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

evidence_text:
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.

Common prednisone side effects:
The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related. They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Serious prednisone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of infection, such as fever, chills, sore throat, cough or a wound that is not healing, since prednisone can hide the usual warning signs;
- blurred vision, eye pain or seeing halos around lights, which can be signs of glaucoma (raised pressure in the eye) or cataracts;

If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

Is prednisone a steroid?:

How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

evidence_text:
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands for about one and a quarter to one and a half days, which is why prednisone is described as short-acting compared with steroids such as dexamethasone. This is also why a course of prednisone can affect your blood sugar, your sleep, and your energy for longer than the drug is measurable in your blood.
Why has my doctor prescribed prednisone every other day?:
Alternate day dosing means taking twice your usual daily dose every other morning instead of a dose every day. It is used for people who need steroid treatment for a long time. Giving your body a day off from the steroid lets your adrenal glands recover between doses, which reduces the risk of adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, withdrawal symptoms, and slowed growth in children.

evidence_text:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.

evidence_text:
Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.

The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.

subject: Rosuvastatin
relation_definition: The subject drug was approved by the US FDA in the year specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

subject: Rosuvastatin
relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
evidence_text:
Common side effects:
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.
Serious side effects:
Rosuvastatin may cause serious side effects, including:
- Muscle pain, tenderness and weakness (myopathy). Muscle problems, including muscle breakdown, can be serious in some people and rarely cause kidney damage that can lead to death. Tell your doctor right away if: you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you have a fever or feel more tired than usual, while you take this medicine. you have muscle problems that do not go away even after your doctor has told you to stop taking this medicine. Your doctor may do further tests to diagnose the cause of your muscle problems. Your chances of getting muscle problems are higher if you: are taking certain other medicines while you take rosuvastatin are 65 years of age or older are of Asian descent have thyroid problems (hypothyroidism) that are not controlled have kidney problems are taking higher doses of this medicine

subject: Rosuvastatin
relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
- Liver problems. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following symptoms of liver problems: feel unusually tired or weak loss of appetite upper belly pain dark urine yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes
- Protein and blood in the urine. Rosuvastatin may cause you to have protein and blood in your urine. If you develop protein or blood in your urine, your doctor may decrease your dose.
- Increase in blood sugar (glucose) levels. Rosuvastatin may cause an increase in your blood sugar levels.
Additional side effects that have been reported with rosuvastatin include abdominal pain, dizziness, memory loss and confusion.
Tell your doctor if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away.
These are not all the possible side effects. For more information, ask your doctor or pharmacist.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

subject: Rosuvastatin
object: may increase risk of muscle problems
relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Tell your doctor about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Also tell the doctor who prescribes rosuvastatin if another doctor increases the dose of another medicine you are taking. Rosuvastatin may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect how rosuvastatin works. Especially tell your doctor if you take:
- coumarin anticoagulants (medicines that prevent blood clots, such as warfarin)
- antacids (medicines you take for heartburn that contain aluminum and magnesium hydroxide)
Taking rosuvastatin with certain medicines may increase the risk of muscle problems. Especially tell your doctor if you take:
- cyclosporine (a medicine for your immune system)
- teriflunomide (a medicine used to treat relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis)
- enasidenib (a medicine used to treat acute myeloid leukemia)
- capmatinib (a medicine for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer)
- fostamatinib (a medicine used to treat low platelet counts)

subject: Rosuvastatin
object: fatty deposits in blood vessel walls
relation_definition: The subject drug is used to decrease or lessen the condition or symptom specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin is used:
- to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.
- along with diet and exercise to lower the level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) cholesterol or "bad" cholesterol: in adults with primary hypercholesterolemia. and slow the buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of blood vessels in adults. in adults and children 8 years of age and older with high blood cholesterol due to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C). in adults and children 7 years of age and older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C).
- along with diet for the treatment of adults with: primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (an inherited condition that causes high levels of cholesterol and fat). hypertriglyceridemia.

subject: Rosuvastatin
relation_definition: The subject drug is used to prevent or lower the risk of the medical event or condition specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

subject: Rosuvastatin
relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver.
Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily.
Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.
Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk. There is no generic semaglutide available. Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic.
Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

subject: Semaglutide
relation_definition: The subject drug is a member of the pharmacological or therapeutic drug class specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Semaglutide works by:
- Stimulates insulin production in the pancreas
- Reduces sugar production in the liver
- Slows down digestion, so food stays in the stomach longer
- Decreases appetite and food intake
These combined actions help you feel full longer, eat less, and maintain better control over blood sugar levels. As a result, semaglutide supports weight loss, improves blood sugar management, and helps reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.
Semaglutide's mechanism of action mimics a natural hormone in the body called GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), which is released after eating to help regulate appetite and blood sugar levels.
The way semaglutide works for kidney-related risk reduction is not fully understood.
Semaglutide belongs to the drug class called GLP-1 receptor agonists.

evidence_text:
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation. For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation. For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.

subject: Semaglutide
relation_definition: The subject drug was approved by the US FDA in the year specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver.
Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily.
Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.
Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk. There is no generic semaglutide available. Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic.
Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

evidence_text:
Ozempic Dosing Information:
Ozempic Injection Recommended Dosage:
- Start Ozempic with a 0.25 mg subcutaneous injection (injection under the skin) once weekly for 4 weeks. The 0.25 mg dosage is intended for treatment initiation and is not effective for glycemic control.
- After 4 weeks on the 0.25 mg dosage, increase the dosage to 0.5 mg once weekly.
- If additional glycemic control is needed after at least 4 weeks on the 0.5 mg dosage, the dosage may be increased to 1 mg once weekly.
- If additional glycemic control is needed after at least 4 weeks on the 1 mg dosage, the dosage may be increased to 2 mg once weekly. The maximum recommended dosage is 2 mg once weekly.
- Administer Ozempic once weekly, on the same day each week, at any time of the day, with or without meals.
- The day of weekly administration can be changed if necessary, as long as the time between two doses is at least 2 days (>48 hours).

Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.
Stomach or gastrointestinal side effects are common, but they tend to be mild and clear up in a few weeks and usually will not interfere with long-term treatment. Stomach side effects can be more common with higher doses.
Tips for managing stomach side effects:
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
- Eat more slowly
- Eat smaller meals
- Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
- Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
- Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
- Do not lie down right after eating
- Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
- If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach

evidence_text:
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation. For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation. For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.

Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.

Tips for managing stomach side effects:
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
- Eat more slowly
- Eat smaller meals
- Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
- Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
- Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
- Do not lie down right after eating
- Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
- If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach

evidence_text:
Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver.
Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily.
Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.
Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk. There is no generic semaglutide available. Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic.
Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

evidence_text:
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation. For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation. For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.

subject: Semaglutide
relation_definition: The subject drug produces its therapeutic effect through the biological mechanism specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver.
Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily.
Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.
Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk. There is no generic semaglutide available. Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic.
Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

evidence_text:
Wegovy injection dosing information:
Initiate Wegovy injection with a dose of 0.25 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly and follow the dose escalation schedule below to minimize gastrointestinal adverse reactions.
Initial Wegovy Injection Dose Escalation Schedule (all indications):
- Week 1 to week 4: 0.25mg once a week
- Week 5 to week 8: 0.5mg once a week
- Week 9 to week 12: 1mg once a week
- Week 13 to week 16: 1.7mg once a week
Maintenance injection dose guidance:
Adult weight reduction maintenance dose:
- 1.7 mg or 2.4 mg (recommended) injected subcutaneously once weekly.
- Dose may be increased to 7.2 mg subcutaneously once weekly on patients who tolerate the 2.4 mg dosage for at least 4 weeks and additional weight reduction is clinically indicated.
- Maximum dose 7.2 mg once weekly
- Consider treatment response and tolerability when selecting the maintenance dosage
Pediatric patients' weight reduction maintenance dose (patients aged 12 years and older):
- Either 2.4 mg (recommended) or 1.7 mg once weekly.

evidence_text:
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation. For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation. For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.

evidence_text:
Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.
Stomach or gastrointestinal side effects are common, but they tend to be mild and clear up in a few weeks and usually will not interfere with long-term treatment. Stomach side effects can be more common with higher doses.
Tips for managing stomach side effects:
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
- Eat more slowly
- Eat smaller meals
- Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
- Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
- Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
- Do not lie down right after eating
- Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
- If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach

Semaglutide oral tablets (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) are taken once a day at least 30 minutes before the first food, beverage, or other oral medications of the day with no more than 4 ounces of plain water only. After 30 minutes of taking the tablet, you may eat, drink, or take other oral medicines. Swallow tablets whole. Do not split, crush, or chew tablets.
General semaglutide use:
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injections in case of severe hypoglycemia.
Tell your doctor if you have frequent symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst or urination. Ask your doctor before changing your dose or medication schedule.
Your treatment may also include diet, exercise, weight control, medical tests, and special medical care.

subject: Rybelsus
relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation. For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation. For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.

Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. evidence_text:
Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It is sold under the brand name Zoloft, and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.

evidence_text:
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.

- Medicines broken down by CYP2D6. Sertraline blocks this liver enzyme, so levels of these drugs can rise and doses may need to be lowered. Examples include propafenone, flecainide, atomoxetine, desipramine, dextromethorphan, metoprolol, nebivolol, perphenazine, thioridazine, tolterodine, and venlafaxine.

Taking sertraline late in pregnancy may raise the risk of newborn problems that need longer hospital stays, breathing support, and tube feeding, and of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a serious lung problem. Use in the month before delivery has been linked with a less than two-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth).
Stopping treatment is not automatically the safer choice. In one study of 201 pregnant women with a history of major depression, those who stopped their antidepressant during pregnancy were more likely to relapse than those who continued. This is a decision to make with your doctor.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information on antidepressant use in pregnancy. You can join by calling 1-866-961-2388.

Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.

evidence_text:
Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It is sold under the brand name Zoloft, and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.

evidence_text:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.

Taking sertraline late in pregnancy may raise the risk of newborn problems that need longer hospital stays, breathing support, and tube feeding, and of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a serious lung problem. Use in the month before delivery has been linked with a less than two-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth).
Stopping treatment is not automatically the safer choice. In one study of 201 pregnant women with a history of major depression, those who stopped their antidepressant during pregnancy were more likely to relapse than those who continued. This is a decision to make with your doctor.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information on antidepressant use in pregnancy. You can join by calling 1-866-961-2388.

evidence_text:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.

evidence_text:
Dosing for PMDD. Sertraline can be taken every day of the menstrual cycle, or only during the luteal phase, meaning you start 14 days before your period is due and continue until it starts, then repeat with each cycle. On daily dosing, the dose can go up by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg a day. On luteal phase dosing, the maximum is 100 mg a day, taken as 50 mg for the first 3 days of the dosing cycle and 100 mg for the rest of it.
Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules. These are not used to start treatment or to titrate a dose, because there are no lower capsule strengths. They can be started in someone who has been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week. The recommended capsule dose is 150 mg or 200 mg once a day, and the maximum is 200 mg a day. Because the dose cannot be lowered in steps using capsules alone, coming off treatment requires switching back to another sertraline product.

evidence_text:
The usual starting dose of sertraline is 25 mg or 50 mg once a day, depending on the condition being treated, and the usual treatment range is 50 mg to 200 mg a day. The maximum dose for most conditions is 200 mg a day.
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range or maximum
Depression (MDD), adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 6 to 12 | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 13 to 17 | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
Panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
PMDD, taken every day | 50 mg a day | Up to 150 mg a day
PMDD, taken in the luteal phase only | 50 mg a day | Up to 100 mg a day
If the starting dose is not enough, the dose can be raised in steps of 25 mg to 50 mg a day. Because sertraline stays in the body for about 24 hours, doses are usually changed no more often than once a week.

evidence_text:
Several medicines interact with sertraline. Give a full list of everything you take to any provider who treats you. The most important interactions are:
- MAOIs. Taking sertraline with an MAOI raises the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the combination is contraindicated. Examples include selegiline, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, phenelzine, linezolid, and methylene blue.
- Pimozide. Sertraline raises pimozide levels, which can lead to QTc prolongation and irregular heartbeats. The combination is contraindicated.
- Other medicines that raise serotonin. These add to the risk of serotonin syndrome. Examples include other SSRIs and SNRIs, triptans for migraine, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids, lithium, tryptophan, buspirone, amphetamines, and St. John's wort.
- Blood thinners and antiplatelet medicines. Aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, and warfarin can add to the bleeding risk. If you take warfarin, your INR should be monitored carefully.

evidence_text:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.

Anyone taking sertraline should be watched closely for worsening symptoms and for new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, thoughts, or feelings, especially in the first few months of treatment and whenever the dose is changed. Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.

evidence_text:
Sertraline is FDA-approved to treat six conditions in adults:
- Major depressive disorder (MDD), the clinical term for depression.
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), where unwanted thoughts drive repeated behaviors.
- Panic disorder, which causes sudden attacks of intense fear along with physical symptoms.
- Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which can follow a frightening or traumatic event.
- Social anxiety disorder (SAD), also called social phobia.
- Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe form of premenstrual symptoms.
In children and teenagers, sertraline is approved only for OCD, from age 6 upward. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 6 years of age, or in children and teenagers for any condition other than OCD.
Not every sertraline product is approved for all six conditions:
- Sertraline tablets and oral solution are approved for all of them.
- Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules are approved only for depression in adults and for OCD in adults and children aged 6 and over.

Dosing for PMDD. Sertraline can be taken every day of the menstrual cycle, or only during the luteal phase, meaning you start 14 days before your period is due and continue until it starts, then repeat with each cycle. On daily dosing, the dose can go up by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg a day. Because the dose cannot be lowered in steps using capsules alone, coming off treatment requires switching back to another sertraline product.

evidence_text:
Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It is sold under the brand name Zoloft, and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.

subject: sertraline
relation_definition: The subject drug is typically taken for the length of time specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.

Taking sertraline late in pregnancy may raise the risk of newborn problems that need longer hospital stays, breathing support, and tube feeding, and of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a serious lung problem. Use in the month before delivery has been linked with a less than two-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth).
Stopping treatment is not automatically the safer choice. In one study of 201 pregnant women with a history of major depression, those who stopped their antidepressant during pregnancy were more likely to relapse than those who continued. This is a decision to make with your doctor.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information on antidepressant use in pregnancy. You can join by calling 1-866-961-2388.

OCD, adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 6 to 12 | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day

Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It is sold under the brand name Zoloft, and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.

Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.

subject: sertraline
relation_definition: In case of an overdose of the subject drug the patient should follow the instruction specified by the object entity.
evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Effects reported after a sertraline tablet overdose include seizures, which may be delayed, and changes in mental state including coma. Heart effects can also be delayed and include changes in the electrical activity of the heart (QRS and QTc prolongation). High blood pressure is seen most often, and low blood pressure is rare, though it can happen when other substances including alcohol have also been taken. Serotonin syndrome can occur, and the risk is higher when several drugs that raise serotonin have been taken together.

subject: sertraline
relation_definition: The subject drug carries the warning specified by the object entity regarding use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
evidence_text:
Taking sertraline late in pregnancy may raise the risk of newborn problems that need longer hospital stays, breathing support, and tube feeding, and of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a serious lung problem. Use in the month before delivery has been linked with a less than two-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth).
Stopping treatment is not automatically the safer choice. In one study of 201 pregnant women with a history of major depression, those who stopped their antidepressant during pregnancy were more likely to relapse than those who continued. This is a decision to make with your doctor.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information on antidepressant use in pregnancy. You can join by calling 1-866-961-2388.

evidence_text:
Dosing for PMDD. Sertraline can be taken every day of the menstrual cycle, or only during the luteal phase, meaning you start 14 days before your period is due and continue until it starts, then repeat with each cycle. On daily dosing, the dose can go up by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg a day. On luteal phase dosing, the maximum is 100 mg a day, taken as 50 mg for the first 3 days of the dosing cycle and 100 mg for the rest of it.
Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules. These are not used to start treatment or to titrate a dose, because there are no lower capsule strengths. They can be started in someone who has been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week. The recommended capsule dose is 150 mg or 200 mg once a day, and the maximum is 200 mg a day. Because the dose cannot be lowered in steps using capsules alone, coming off treatment requires switching back to another sertraline product.

evidence_text: Older adults clear sertraline more slowly. In one study, plasma clearance in people aged 65 and over was about 40% lower than in adults aged 25 to 32, so it took 2 to 3 weeks to reach steady levels rather than about 1 week. Doctors usually start older adults at the low end of the dose range. Older adults are also at greater risk of low sodium levels in the blood, particularly if they take diuretics (water pills) or are dehydrated.

evidence_text:
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.

evidence_text:
It is not known whether this risk continues beyond about four months of treatment. There is good evidence that antidepressants delay depression coming back in adults, and depression itself raises the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
Anyone taking sertraline should be watched closely for worsening symptoms and for new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, thoughts, or feelings, especially in the first few months of treatment and whenever the dose is changed. Call your healthcare provider right away, or call 911 in an emergency, if you notice:
- thoughts about suicide or dying, or attempts to harm yourself
- new or worse depression, anxiety, or panic attacks
- feeling agitated, restless, angry, or irritable
- acting aggressive or violent, or acting on dangerous impulses
- trouble sleeping
- a big increase in activity or talking more than is normal for you
- any other unusual change in behavior or mood
Tell family members or caregivers which symptoms to watch for, so they can call your provider if you are not able to.

evidence_text:
It is not known whether this risk continues beyond about four months of treatment. There is good evidence that antidepressants delay depression coming back in adults, and depression itself raises the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
Anyone taking sertraline should be watched closely for worsening symptoms and for new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, thoughts, or feelings, especially in the first few months of treatment and whenever the dose is changed. Call your healthcare provider right away, or call 911 in an emergency, if you notice:
- thoughts about suicide or dying, or attempts to harm yourself
- new or worse depression, anxiety, or panic attacks
- feeling agitated, restless, angry, or irritable
- acting aggressive or violent, or acting on dangerous impulses
- trouble sleeping
- a big increase in activity or talking more than is normal for you
- any other unusual change in behavior or mood
Tell family members or caregivers which symptoms to watch for, so they can call your provider if you are not able to.

Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.

evidence_text:
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%

evidence_text:
Take sertraline exactly as prescribed, once a day, in either the morning or the evening. Take it at around the same time each day.
- Tablets and capsules can be taken with or without food. Taking sertraline with food causes only a small increase in the amount absorbed.
- Swallow capsules whole. Do not open, crush, or chew them.
- Your doctor may start you on a low dose and raise it gradually, usually no more often than once a week.
- Keep taking sertraline even if you feel well, and do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
- Tell any doctor or lab that you take sertraline before you have tests. Sertraline can cause a false-positive result on urine screening tests for benzodiazepines, and this can continue for several days after you stop taking it. A confirmatory test will tell the difference.
- Store sertraline at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C).
How to take sertraline oral solution:
Sertraline oral solution must be diluted before you take it. Do not mix it in advance.
